title: The Wizard, the Goat, and the Magic Doughnut
markdown:
The Whispering Peaks had valleys so green they practically winked, mountains that played peek-a-boo with clouds, and bridges woven from vines so old they hummed with tales. Market ledges clung to the rock like pockets: shiny trinkets that winked like captured stars, potions that fizzed with forgotten giggles, fruits so plump they tasted of sunshine and sweet dreams. Wizard Leopold’s beard sometimes smelled faintly of singed sugar plums. Don’t ask. His coin purse, usually as fat and happy as a well-fed griffin (a creature he rather admired), was as flat and sad as a deflated balloon. His tummy was performing a grand opera of hunger. Ooooooh, the hunger, it wailed, quite without dignity.

“Quip, my dearest feather-mutt,” Leopold murmured, pointy hat giving a wobbly lean. “A proper supper is urgently needed. Our money has taken a rather extended holiday.”

Quip, a clever jackdaw, ruffled shiny black feathers like old parchment. Beady eyes, obsidian chips. “Caw. Broke. Very broke.” He sounded like a tiny grumpy man complaining about the price of seeds.

“Precisely. One cannot do important spell-casting on an empty stomach. Terribly inefficient. A bit undignified.” Being broke was, in Leopold’s expert opinion, a perfectly fashionable wizardly hobby. Therefore they needed coin, and they needed it without the whole Lower Ledge knowing they were skint.

The plan: they would head to the market on the Lower Ledge. Leopold, with charming smile and twinkly eyes, would amuse the vendors. Quip, being the zippy one, would dazzle—perhaps a spectacular loop-de-loop. Coins would flutter, dropped by astonished shoppers or whisked by a magically conjured gust. Grand presentation. You’ve got to put on a show.

They went down, down, down a series of wonderfully wobbly rainbow-coloured steps carved into the mountain. Quip zipped ahead with a triumphant Caw, a black blur against vibrant flowers and shimmering moss. The air buzzed with barter and spice. A stall overflowing with glimmering goblets belonged to Madame Grizelda, stout, apron embroidered with mischievous sprites, voice a friendly thunderstorm. She was already haggling.

“This goblet holds three precious drops of morning dew from the highest peak,” she boomed. “And it will whisper secrets of the stars into its owner’s ear.”

A nervous gnome with a drooping hat peered. “How much for celestial secrets?”

“A mere ten sun-spun coins.”

Leopold winced a private wince. He needed five for shepherd’s pie and berry tea. He edged closer, a casual admirer of exquisite wares.

But a loud unmistakable Baaaah erupted from behind a wobbly stack of enchanted rugs. Bartholomew the goat, whose gift was appearing at the exact moment you wished to melt into cobblestones, munched sad mountain moss. He blinked intelligent bewildered eyes at Leopold, then Quip, then Leopold. Another Baaaah that sounded suspiciously like, Looking a bit peckish, aren’t we? Then, with the air of an important diplomat, he nudged a loose coin from Madame Grizelda’s till. It clattered across stone and landed beside Leopold’s boot.

Therefore Leopold’s heart became a woodpecker. Grizelda’s head snapped. “Is that my coin rolling about?”

“Not at all, Madame. An enthusiastic member of the local fauna. The sheer spontaneity of mountain life.” He scooped the coin with hungry-wizard speed. “A most fine specimen. Very observant.”

Bartholomew bleated a suppressed snicker and contemplated a crack in the rock. Grizelda was thankfully stolen by a new customer. One coin. Not enough for a plump sausage. The only witness: a goat with a doctorate in inopportune timing.

Then the sky, which had been cheerful blue, decided to weep. Fat drops sent vendors scurrying. Leopold and Quip ducked under an empty tea stall that smelled of dried lavender and roasted barley.

Rain tapped a gentle rhythm against the pane, little shimmering rivers on the glass. Quip perched calmly, glossy feathers gleaming. “Do you remember how we met? Properly met,” Leopold said, fond, not lecturing. “You a scrawny rather indignant fledgling, all ruffled feathers, trying to pilfer cheese. Admirable ambition. Then Bartholomew arrived and nibbled the rope on a display of remarkably unstable jam jars. Chaos, absolute delicious chaos. You didn’t flee. You defended that cheese. He distracted the vendor just long enough. I knew then: fierce, resourceful, and perfectly capable of dealing with goats.” Quip nudged his beak against Leopold’s cheek. Leopold watched Bartholomew through the wet glass, still being present, which was the goat’s entire career. After the jam, everyone had called him a menace. Leopold had seen unwavering commitment to simply being there. “Not a pet. A perspective. A very stubborn perspective, perhaps, but a perspective.”

The rain softened. Gold light broke through. Therefore Leopold had an idea, peculiar and entirely his.

“The village celebration. The talent showcase. I shall perform. Bartholomew shall be my unwitting, utterly essential co-star.”

Evening descended. The village of Oakhaven, nestled in a verdant cozy curve of valley, began to glow. Lanterns strung between sturdy oaks. Stalls laden with pies fragrant with cinnamon and apples. Steaming mugs of spiced cider. Laughter as light as dancing fireflies. Leopold, surprisingly dapper in his best robes (free of recent scorch marks, a minor miracle), stood beside a small wonderfully wobbly makeshift stage. Quip, perched regally, looked exceptionally smug. Bartholomew, remarkably clean, a garland of wildflowers jauntily round his neck, stood patiently and occasionally nudged Leopold’s leg as if to say he had been practising his best bleat.

“Esteemed villagers. ‘The Dance of the Disappearing Doughnut.’”

A hush. Children leaned, eyes wide. Bartholomew, slightly bewildered but game, followed every intricate movement. Leopold performed almost invisible magical gestures. Quip, with perfect timing, let out sharp precise caws like tiny bursts of concentrated magic. Leopold conjured a plump sugary doughnut, made it wobble seductively, then with a flourish made it vanish. Poof. The villagers murmured in pleasant confusion. At the peak of intrigue Leopold pointed dramatically at Bartholomew. The goat, startled, took a curious step, and with a perfect innocent Baaaah a single perfectly formed golden-brown sugary doughnut materialized on the tip of his nose.

The square erupted. Not grand world-shattering magic. Not complex spells. Charming, utterly silly, a wave of unadulterated delight. Children giggled. Adults chuckled. The joy was as palpable as lantern heat. By the time the performance concluded, Bartholomew having “eaten” several more magically conjured doughnuts that appeared with puffs of sugary steam, Leopold found a small respectable pile of coins at his feet, glistening in the light.

Later that evening, coin purse comfortably replenished, a hearty supper of shepherd’s pie and steaming berry tea waited in Leopold’s cozy cottage. Outside, rain returned, tapping a lullaby on the pane. Inside: fire-glow, good company, Quip counting nothing because he had already been paid in cheese-memory, Bartholomew nested in a soft pile of straw with a long contented sigh. Leopold’s purse was no longer a deflated balloon. The doughnut on the goat’s nose had been the whole trick. The mountain, for once, did not ask for ten sun-spun coins, and the tummy’s grand opera took a well-earned interval.
characters: Leopold (broke wizard with a singed-sugar-plum beard), Quip (a clever jackdaw)
audience: children aged 9-10, amusing distant-lands fantasy for independent readers
author: StoryGen Community
